tagline: A moray that changes colour as it grows
summary: A ribbon-thin moray with flared, leaf-like nostrils that peers from sand and rubble burrows near coral reefs. It is the only moray known to change colour abruptly as it ages — black as a juvenile, electric blue, then yellow — a sequence long thought to track a change of sex.

facts.title: Black, then blue, then yellow
facts.text: Small juveniles are jet black with a yellow dorsal fin. Males are bright blue with a yellow snout and jaw, and females are yellow, sometimes with blue towards the tail.

facts.title: A one-off among morays
facts.text: It is the only moray eel known to go through abrupt colour changes as it grows.

facts.title: Male first, then female?
facts.text: Ribbon eels are widely described as switching sex from male to female (protandry). But this has been inferred from their colour changes and not yet confirmed directly.

facts.title: Enormous nostrils
facts.text: The tip of its snout carries enormous, flared nostrils — one of the features that makes this slender eel so striking.

facts.title: Head-out ambusher
facts.text: Secretive by nature, it usually hides in sand or rubble near reefs, often with only its head sticking out, and feeds on small fishes.

notes: Sex change: Fishes of Australia states it as fact, but FishBase explicitly says 'Protandry is diagnosed based on colouration, but not confirmed' — so presented as hypothesis and no 'reproduction' category assigned. No allowed category clearly fits, so categories is empty. Depth: FishBase 1–67 m (Fishes of Australia gives 1–57 m). Gallery photo location not given on Commons.
